title: Noun plurals
explanation: Most nouns just add -s: livro → livros, mãe → mães. Nouns ending in -ão usually become -ões (estação → estações), but a few take -ães (pão → pães) or -ãos (irmão → irmãos). Words ending in -l change it to -is (hotel → hotéis, animal → animais), and words ending in -r or -z add -es (mulher → mulheres).

examples.pt: Eu comprei dois pães na padaria.
examples.en: I bought two rolls at the bakery.

examples.pt: Os hotéis do centro são caros.

examples.en: The women are in the garden.

mistake.en: There are lots of hotels here.
mistake.reason: Nouns ending in -l drop it and add -is in the plural.

title: Adjective agreement and position
pattern: noun + adjective, matching gender and number: a casa branca · os carros novos
explanation: Adjectives match their noun in gender and number: o carro novo, a casa nova, os carros novos. They normally come after the noun. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant (grande, feliz, azul) have the same form for masculine and feminine. A few common ones like bom and grande often go before the noun.

mistake.wrong: Eu moro em uma branca casa.
mistake.right: Eu moro em uma casa branca.
mistake.en: I live in a white house.
mistake.reason: Colors and most other adjectives come after the noun.

title: Subject pronouns, você and a gente
pattern: eu · você · ele/ela · a gente / nós · vocês · eles/elas
explanation: In Brazil, você (you) and vocês (you all) are the normal ways to say 'you', and they take the same verb form as ele/eles. In speech, a gente (literally 'the people') is very common for 'we' and takes the ele form: a gente vai, not a gente vamos. Nós is also used and takes its own form (nós vamos).

examples.pt: A gente vai à praia amanhã.
examples.en: We're going to the beach tomorrow.

mistake.reason: A gente means 'we' but takes the same verb form as ele/ela.

title: Present tense of regular verbs
pattern: -ar: falo, fala, falamos, falam · -er: como, come, comemos, comem · -ir: abro, abre, abrimos, abrem
explanation: Drop -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for the person: eu -o, você/ele/a gente -a or -e, nós -amos/-emos/-imos, vocês/eles -am or -em. The present covers both 'I speak' and 'I'm speaking' as well as habits.

examples.en: She eats a lot of fruit.

examples.pt: Nós abrimos a loja às nove.
examples.en: We open the store at nine.

mistake.reason: The verb must be conjugated; the infinitive alone doesn't say who does it.

title: Tem = there is / there are
explanation: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, tem (from ter, to have) means both 'has' and 'there is/there are'. Há means the same thing but sounds more formal or written. The form doesn't change for plurals: tem um banco, tem dois bancos.

examples.en: Is there a pharmacy near here?
There are a lot of people at the beach.
There's no milk in the fridge.

mistake.en: There's a bank on the corner.
mistake.reason: To say something exists somewhere, use tem, not estar.

title: de and em + article
pattern: de + o/a = do/da · em + o/a = no/na · em + um/uma = num/numa
explanation: The prepositions de (of, from) and em (in, on, at) combine with a following article: do, da, dos, das; no, na, nos, nas. This is required, not optional. Before city names without an article you just use de or em: de Boston, em São Paulo, but do Rio, no Brasil.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

examples.pt: Eu moro em São Paulo, perto da praça.
examples.en: I live in São Paulo, near the square.

mistake.wrong: A chave está em a mesa.
mistake.en: The key is on the table.
mistake.reason: Em and a always merge into na.

title: Possessives: meu, seu, dele
explanation: Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: minha casa (my house) even if you're a man. In Brazil, seu/sua usually means 'your' (of você), so for 'his' and 'her' people say o carro dele and a casa dela, placed after the noun. An article before the possessive (o meu carro) is optional.

mistake.reason: The possessive agrees with casa, which is feminine, so it's minha.

title: Este, esse, aquele
explanation: In spoken Brazilian Portuguese, esse and este are used almost interchangeably for 'this' or 'that' near the speaker or listener; esse is far more common. Aquele is for things farther away. Isso, isto and aquilo are neutral forms for ideas or unnamed things: o que é isso?

examples.en: That building over there is a hotel.

mistake.reason: With a named noun use esse/essa; the neutral form is isso, never esso.

title: Question words
pattern: (o) que · quem · onde · quando · como · quanto · qual · por que
explanation: Question words usually go at the start, and the word order stays like a statement: Onde você mora? A yes/no question is just a statement with rising intonation: Você é brasileiro? Quanto agrees with the noun (quantos anos, quantas pessoas), and por que (why) is answered with porque (because).

mistake.en: How many people are at the party?
mistake.reason: Quanto agrees with the noun it counts, here feminine plural pessoas.

title: Negation with não
explanation: Put não right before the verb: eu não sei. With nada, ninguém and nunca after the verb, não is still needed: não tem nada. In speech Brazilians often add a second não at the end for emphasis (não sei não), and in short answers just repeat the verb: Você quer? Quero / Não quero.

mistake.reason: When nada comes after the verb, the verb still needs não.

title: Gostar de
pattern: gostar de + noun / infinitive (do, da, de …)
explanation: Gostar (to like) always needs de before what is liked, and de merges with articles: gosto do Rio, gosto da praia. Before an infinitive it's just de: gosto de cozinhar. A short answer to 'Do you like…?' is simply Gosto or Não gosto.

mistake.reason: Gostar always takes de before the thing you like.

title: Estar + gerund (present continuous)
explanation: For something happening right now, Brazilians use estar plus the gerund: falar → falando, comer → comendo, dormir → dormindo. (In Portugal people say está a falar, but in Brazil the gerund is standard.)

mistake.reason: Brazilian Portuguese uses the gerund (-ando) after estar, not a + infinitive.

title: Telling time
pattern: Que horas são? · É uma hora · São duas (horas) · às três = at three
explanation: Use é for one o'clock, noon and midnight (é uma hora, é meio-dia) and são for everything else (são duas, são dez e meia). 'At' a time is à/às: à uma, às oito. Hours use feminine numbers: uma, duas.

examples.pt: Que horas são? São duas e meia.
examples.en: What time is it? It's two thirty.

mistake.reason: Every hour except one o'clock, noon and midnight is plural, so it takes são.

title: Going somewhere: ir a / ir para
pattern: ir + a/para + place (ao, à, pro, pra)
explanation: With ir, the destination takes a or para. A merges with the article (ao cinema, à praia), and para is often shortened in speech to pra, pro (pra praia, pro centro). Para tends to suggest staying longer, but in everyday speech pra is the most common choice. Don't use em with ir.

examples.pt: A gente vai pra praia amanhã.
examples.en: We're going to the beach tomorrow.

examples.pt: Ela vai para o Rio nas férias.
examples.en: She's going to Rio on vacation.

mistake.reason: Ir no is very common in casual speech, but the standard preposition with ir is a or para.

title: Past tense of regular verbs
pattern: -ar: falei, falou, falamos, falaram · -er: comi, comeu · -ir: abri, abriu
explanation: The pretérito perfeito describes completed actions: I spoke, I ate. Eu forms end in -ei or -i, and você/ele/a gente forms in -ou, -eu or -iu. The nós form of -ar and -ir verbs looks like the present (falamos), so context or words like ontem make the time clear.

examples.pt: Ela comeu uma salada no almoço.
examples.en: She ate a salad for lunch.
Did you all watch the movie?

mistake.reason: The eu form of an -ar verb in the past ends in -ei; -ou is for você/ele.
